claims.text: The target alloy is equimolar WTaTiVZr.
WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten will both be microstructurally characterized before testing.
High-temperature in-situ TEM straining combined with complementary mechanical testing can compare deformation in WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten.
Temperatures of 1000–1300 °C are representative of high-temperature plasma-facing-component service.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has severe or high-density lattice distortion.
The constituent elements responsible for the distortion in WTaTiVZr are relatively low-activation elements.
Lattice distortion produces an altered dislocation network in WTaTiVZr.
Severe lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr restricts dislocation cross-slip.
Restricted cross-slip forces WTaTiVZr to activate more homogeneous dislocation nucleation and motion.
More homogeneous dislocation activity delays strain localization and crack initiation in WTaTiVZr.
Pure tungsten deforms through dominant dislocation channeling and early strain localization under the proposed conditions.
Features of dislocation behavior in pure BCC tungsten can be unfavorable to ductility.
WTaTiVZr will develop a higher density of more uniformly distributed dislocations than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will have a higher yield strain than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will sustain more plastic deformation before failure than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will have higher toughness than pure tungsten under identical elevated-temperature test conditions.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism will dominate under plasma-facing-component-relevant high-temperature conditions.
In-situ TEM artifacts and differences between nanoscale and bulk behavior may limit interpretation of the comparison.
The mechanistic rationale is based on analogies to other high-entropy alloys and refractory metals rather than direct evidence on WTaTiVZr.
The quantitative toughness enhancement and the translation from in-situ behavior to bulk performance are uncertain.

contradictions.description: Micro-pillar compression is presented as a complementary bulk test, although it is a microscale test. Thus, the stated design does not necessarily support the prediction that the mechanism will be confirmed in both nanoscale and bulk mechanical tests.
